summary: This standards-track memo defines the Content-Disposition header field for MIME messages, which conveys presentation information such as whether a body part should display inline or be treated as an attachment.

eli5.summary: A label on each piece of mail saying show this now or save for later.

questions: how does the filename parameter work in mime
is it safe to trust the content-disposition filename
subtitle: The mail header that tells a mail program whether to show a part now or offer it as an attachment.

tldr.problem: MIME describes what a message part contains but not how the sender wants it presented, leaving that entirely to the mail program.
tldr.mechanism: The optional Content-Disposition header marks a part as inline or attachment, and can add parameters such as filename, creation-date, modification-date, read-date and size.
tldr.outcome: It revises the Experimental RFC 1806, and has since been updated by RFC 2184 and RFC 2231, which handle long and non-ASCII parameter values.

today: RFC 2183 is a Proposed Standard that replaces the Experimental RFC 1806. It has been updated by RFC 2184 and RFC 2231, so read those for long or non-ASCII parameter values.

sections.title: Why a Presentation Header
sections.content:
MIME gives a standard way to pack several pieces of data into one message, but it leaves presentation to the mail user agent (MUA). Two common styles are a main document with a list of separate attachments, and a single document with every part displayed inline. An attachment normally needs a positive action from the recipient, while inline parts are displayed automatically.

The Content-Disposition header lets the sender tag each part with its desired presentation. It also allows a suggested filename and the preservation of file dates when a file travels by MIME mail. This memo revises the Experimental protocol of RFC 1806.
sections.eli5: Mail programs have to guess whether to show a picture or hide it. This sticker lets the sender say what they want.

sections.title: The Header Field
sections.content:
Content-Disposition is optional and valid for any MIME entity. If it is absent, the MUA may use whatever presentation method it deems suitable. The syntax is the field name, a disposition type (inline, attachment or an extension token; values are not case-sensitive), then any number of ;-separated parameters.

Date parameters hold a quoted RFC 822 date-time and MUST use numeric time zones. A short parameter value of 78 characters or fewer made only of non-tspecials characters SHOULD be a plain token; a short ASCII value that includes tspecials SHOULD be a quoted-string. Values longer than 78 characters, or containing non-ASCII characters, MUST be encoded as specified in RFC 2184.
sections.eli5: The sticker has a main word, then optional extra notes after semicolons, like the file name.

sections.title: Inline and Attachment
sections.content:
A body part should be marked inline if it is meant to be displayed automatically when the message is displayed, in the order in which the parts occur.

A part marked attachment is separate from the main body, and its display should not be automatic but contingent on some further action by the user. A MUA might show a bitmap terminal user an icon, or a character terminal user a list of attachments to choose from.

On a multipart body part, the header applies to the multipart as a whole. With attachment, presentation should not proceed without explicit user action; once the user chooses to view it, the subparts' own dispositions are consulted. With inline, the multipart is displayed normally, but an attachment subpart still needs user action. The header may also be used on the main body of an RFC 822 message.
sections.eli5: Inline means 'open this now'. Attachment means 'here is a package; open it if you want'.

sections.title: Filename, Dates and Size
sections.content:
The filename parameter suggests a name if the part is stored in a file. The receiving MUA must not use it blindly: it SHOULD check that the name fits local filesystem conventions, does not overwrite an existing file and is not a security problem. The MUA SHOULD NOT respect any directory path in it and should treat it as a terminal component only. Its presence does not force the part to be written to a file, so it may be used even on inline parts.

The creation-date, modification-date and read-date parameters MAY record those dates of the file, as quoted RFC 822 date-times. The RFC warns that the UNIX st_ctime attribute is not the file's creation time. The size parameter gives an approximate size in octets, for example to pre-allocate space.
sections.eli5: The sticker can suggest a name for the saved file and when it was made or changed, but the receiver should check the name is safe first.

sections.title: Unknown Values and New Registrations
sections.content:
Unrecognized parameters should be ignored. Unrecognized disposition types should be treated as attachment, because a sender who bothers to define a new type is more likely aiming for something more elaborate than inline display. Unless noted otherwise, parameters are valid for all dispositions.

New disposition values (besides inline and attachment) may be defined only by Internet standards-track documents, or by Experimental documents approved by the Internet Engineering Steering Group. New parameters are registered with IANA by sending a short template by email.
sections.eli5: If a mail program sees a sticker it does not know, it plays safe and treats the part as a package to open later.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples. The first is a JPEG marked inline that is shown at once. The second is a JPEG marked attachment with a suggested file name genome.jpeg and a modification-date parameter.

The third nests multiparts. The user sees text-part-1 immediately, then must take action to view multipart-2. After that, text-part-2 shows right away, and the user must act again to view jpeg-1.
sections.eli5: A picture marked 'inline' pops up. A picture marked 'attachment' waits in a list until you click it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it does not change the status quo for exchanging data, except that a sender can now suggest a filename. A receiving MUA must make sure that name is not a hazard. On UNIX the RFC lists creating startup files such as .login, creating or overwriting system files such as /etc/passwd, overwriting any existing file, placing executables in a command search path, and sending the file to a pipe.

In general the MUA should not name or place the file so that it is interpreted or executed without the user explicitly starting that action. The list is only a set of examples, and implementors must watch for hazards on their own systems.
sections.eli5: A sender could suggest a sneaky file name, like one that overwrites an important file. The mail program must never trust the name without checking.
